title: Tanmaxxing: The Viral Tanning Trend Dermatologists Say Is Skin Cancer Waiting to Happen
excerpt: Gen Z influencers are encouraging extreme UV exposure without sunscreen, driving a surge in misinformation that medical experts warn could fuel a skin cancer crisis.
body:
• Tanmaxxing, a social media trend encouraging extreme UV exposure without sunscreen, has surged among Gen Z users on TikTok and Instagram, alarming dermatologists worldwide.
  • The American Academy of Dermatology found that 64% of Gen Z respondents had encountered sunscreen misinformation online, and 20% said getting a tan was more important than preventing skin cancer.
  • The World Health Organization classifies UV radiation and tanning beds as Group 1 carcinogens — the same category as tobacco and asbestos — and using a tanning bed before age 35 raises melanoma risk by about 75%.

The Trend Dermatologists Are Fighting

A social media trend called "tanmaxxing" is pushing young people to seek out peak ultraviolet exposure in pursuit of darker skin, often while minimizing or skipping sunscreen entirely. Popular on TikTok and Instagram, the trend involves checking the UV index not to avoid the sun but to find the optimal time to tan, sometimes combining hours of direct sunlight with tanning oils, bronzers, and even tanning bed sessions.

The trend has roots in the broader "looksmaxxing" community, which promotes extreme measures to maximize physical attractiveness. Variants include UV maxxing, carrotmaxxing, bronzermaxxing, and sunmaxxing, according to USA Today.

For dermatologists who have spent decades educating the public about skin cancer prevention, the trend represents a troubling reversal.

"A tan isn't a glow-up — it's your skin's visible distress signal that DNA damage has already happened. As a skin cancer specialist, I've taken care of thousands of skin cancers on patients who 'tanmaxxed' before it had a name."

— Dr. Michael Tassavor, board-certified dermatologist, New York

What the Science Says

The medical consensus is unambiguous. "There is no such thing as a healthy tan," said Dr. Mary Wu Chang, associate professor of Dermatology and Pediatrics at UConn Health. "A tan is actually a sign that the skin has been damaged by ultraviolet radiation. Every tan represents injury to the skin's cells and increases the risk of premature aging and skin cancer over time."

When skin is exposed to UV rays, it produces additional melanin — the pigment that gives skin its color — as a damage response. That darkening is not a sign of health but of cellular injury. UV damage accumulates silently over years and can lead to premature aging and multiple forms of skin cancer, including melanoma.

The WHO classifies UV radiation and tanning beds as Group 1 carcinogens, placing them in the same category as tobacco smoking, asbestos, and plutonium. Using a tanning bed before age 35 raises the risk of melanoma by approximately 75%, according to dermatologist Dr. Tassavor. At least one in five Americans will develop skin cancer in their lifetime, per the American Academy of Dermatology.

The Misinformation Problem

A key driver of the trend is online misinformation. The American Academy of Dermatology's 2026 Practice Safe Sun Survey found that 64% of Gen Z respondents had encountered sunscreen misinformation on social media. More than one in three said social media influencers were their primary source of skincare advice, and 20% said getting a tan was more important to them than preventing skin cancer.

Two common beliefs behind tanmaxxing are false, according to medical experts: skipping sunscreen does not produce a "better" tan, and a base tan does not protect skin from future sunburns. A base tan provides minimal UV protection and is itself evidence of damage already sustained.

Dermatologists also emphasize that while people with more melanin have a lower risk of sunburn, everyone is susceptible to UV damage. Skin cancer in people with darker skin tones is often detected later, when the disease has already progressed, according to the American Academy of Dermatology.

A Pattern Familiar to South Asians

The tanmaxxing trend sits at an ironic intersection with colorism in South Asian communities, where lighter skin has historically been prized and dark skin stigmatized. While one part of social media glamorizes extreme tanning, another perpetuates a global skin-lightening industry worth billions.

For South Asian Americans navigating both cultural contexts, dermatologists stress that the science is the same regardless of baseline skin tone: UV exposure causes cumulative cellular damage, and no amount of melanin makes anyone immune to skin cancer.

What Experts Recommend

Dermatologists recommend broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher, reapplied every two hours during sun exposure. Protective clothing, seeking shade during peak UV hours (typically 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.), and avoiding tanning beds remain the standard guidance. For those who want bronzed skin, spray tans and self-tanners are the only methods dermatologists consider safe.

Parents concerned about the trend's influence on teenagers are advised to focus on building critical thinking skills rather than lecturing. Asking questions — Where did you hear about this? Is this person a dermatologist or an influencer? — can be more effective than outright criticism, according to guidance from Bitdefender's digital safety researchers.
